author: Thomas Reese
title: Bishops get educated on Gen Z, who are ‘religious but not spiritual’
original_title: Bishops get educated on Gen Z, who are ‘religious but not spiritual’
summary: (RNS) — ‘For men,’ Vaidyanathan concludes, ‘religiosity has much more to do with identity, with affiliating … with attendance. And for women, it’s much more about the interior life.’
full_content:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

(RNS) — “It’s probably premature to say that there is a Catholic revival taking place,” the U.S. Catholic bishops were told by a panel of experts from The Catholic University of America on Nov. 18 at their annual meeting in Baltimore.

“And while we rejoice in higher numbers of conversions, we cannot help but lament the high number of people who leave the Catholic Church,” continued Aaron Weldon, the panel moderator and director of the New Wineskins project at the Catholic University of America.

According to the Pew Research Center, for every adult convert entering the church, 8.4 adults leave.

The panel was kicked off by sociologist Brandon Vaidyanathan, who, using data from a 2026 Gallup survey, laid out for the bishops how young people (18- to 29-year-olds) are expressing their religious beliefs and identities.

An encouraging finding is that about two-thirds of young Catholics say that religion has grown in importance for them in the past five years compared to 41% of older Catholics. The young Catholics also think that the people around them are becoming more religious.

Vaidyanathan cautions that this is a subjective judgment and that the Pew Research Center in a longitudinal study did not find any increased religious activity (church attendance, prayer life) in this same cohort. Increased interest in religion is not yet reflected in increased religious practice.

Young Catholics are attending church weekly at about the same rate (24% to 25%) as other Catholics but praying significantly less than older Catholics. Of young Catholics, 28% are praying daily or more compared to 48% of older Catholics.

And while the previous generation tended to identify as “spiritual but not religious,” this new generation is more likely to identify as “religious but not spiritual.” This is even more true of young Catholics, 30% of whom consider themselves “religious but not spiritual” versus only 12% for older Catholics. Only 14% of young Catholics consider themselves “spiritual but not religious.”

 

More than half (60%) of those who say that they are “religious but not spiritual” are men. Young men are also more likely to consider themselves neither religious nor spiritual compared to young women.

When Vaidyanathan asks his students about the term “spirituality,” they said, “That’s for my mom and her friends. They go on these yoga retreats. They’re kind of pagan, you know, they like to do these weird, woo rituals. That’s not for us.” This fits with the finding that the “spiritual but not religious” tend to be seeking a sense of inner peace and a connection with their true self rather than a connection with the divine.

Vaidyanathan notes that men and women seem to be equally religious, but that means something somewhat different for each of them. Among those who feel religion has become more important, men attend church weekly at a slightly higher rate than women. Women, on the other hand, are much more likely to pray daily (54% versus 35%).

“For men,” Vaidyanathan concludes, “religiosity has much more to do with identity, with affiliating… with attendance. And for women, it’s much more about the interior life.”

His research also found that 18- to 29-year-olds are much more likely to say, compared to their older peers, that they are yearning for a connection to community and yearning for guidance to tell right from wrong. And young women are yearning more for moral guidance than young men.

And when asked what factors helped young people become more religious, the top five responses were “personal experiences or life events, religious beliefs or teachings, family or social relationships, worship, music, ritual and sacred spaces, and finding beauty in religious spaces or rituals.”

He notes that a Chicago archdiocesan study of OCIA entrants in 20 dioceses found that “it’s the sacred liturgy, prayer, ritual and sacraments that is drawing people towards the church.”

Finally, he noted that the next generation of Catholics is mostly Hispanic, but that they do not attend church as much as others.

His presentation was followed by theologian Angela Franks, who put religious seeking in the context of identity and contemporary culture.

Using concepts first developed by sociologist Zygmunt Bauman, she notes that “in our contemporary moment we privilege things such as fluidity, flexibility and change. And this preference contrasts with premodern societies that valued stability, solidity.”

In premodern, solid societies, our identities are predetermined within solid social structures, whereas in liquid, modern societies, we tend to mistrust solid institutions and must make our own identities.

RELATED: Will the bishops learn how to surf the blue wave?

This can be exhausting and demoralizing, she notes, which can lead to identity politics that “provide very visible identities behind which there’s usually a group of noisy supporters for that identity. As Bauman says, it provides us with an identity suit off-the-rack as opposed to having to sew an identity for ourselves.”

But “because these tend to develop online, these identities tend to be easy to join but also easy to leave.”

“They are often very superficial,” she continues, “because, given that so much of this happens online, it relies on a very visual culture to backstop this identity.”

“Some people love this very liquid nature of identity formation because it’s wrapped up with freedom,” she notes. “Other people are deeply uncomfortable with it.”

Men are more likely than women to yearn for solidity, which “goes along with a growing sense of their being unappreciated in part because of so many traditionally male jobs being technologized and automated.”

“Against the background of our very liquid culture, Christianity looks exceptionally solid,” explains Franks. “Her dogmas are rooted in the divine person of Jesus Christ. She has traditions. She has an ecclesiastical hierarchy. She has an ordered liturgy.”

Franks concludes that this is very likely one driver in the rise of young adult conversions to Catholicism.

But at its beginnings, she reminds the bishops, Christianity was a liquefying force that threatened the solid identities of the time, when what mattered was “whether you’re free or slave, you’re Roman or not Roman, you are wealthy or poor, what kind of family you belong into.” These might have been important, but “the ultimate place where we seek identity in Christianity is in God’s call to the person,” she said.

However, in modern times, when God is removed from the process of creating an identity, the church becomes the enemy of freedom, just another solid institution to rebel against.

“It is understandable,” she says, “that those who are dissatisfied with what the secular and liquid West provides would be attracted to the church.” But she warns that the church is more liquid than they think.

While Catholicism is solidly based on the person of Jesus Christ, who is the revelation of the Father, the magisterium is also guided by the Holy Spirit to work in new historical situations.

“Catholic doctrine is not a malleable language game,” she says. Nor is Catholicism “an antiquarianism which looks to just one age’s practices or language to norm us.”

RELATED: Why I hate the old Latin Mass: A confession

“The church has a strength in flexibility or maybe a flexible strength that enables her to weather storms through history,” she concludes.

What is needed is a “delicate balance between liquidity and solidity that is, in truth, very hard for people to strike and maintain,” she says. “We tend to favor extremes.”

If in response to the contemporary identity crisis, “if people are looking simply for the most solid place to stand,” Franks warns, “they are going to be scandalized when the church proves herself to be less predictable than they were hoping.”

As a result, she says, it is important “to have more careful intellectual formation on the development of doctrine and what it means for practices to grow and change.”

But the problem is not primarily intellectual. It is an existential crisis, she believes. “People have yoked their identity to the church being a certain way.” There is a need to recognize “that my personal foundation is rooted in the triune God and therefore is rooted in his reliable personal love for me, but also that the church is divinely equipped to ride through the vicissitudes of history.”

She concluded with a meditation on the “La Navicella,” a mosaic created by Giotto on the façade of old St. Peter’s in Rome in 1298 and has been reproduced by others. It shows Peter attempting to walk on water to Jesus. Here the solid boat represents the safety of the church, while Peter steps out of the boat to follow Christ into the liquid world.

Peter’s “foolish wish to follow Christ into the liquid is unfathomably granted, at least as long as he has faith in Christ,” says Franks. “This is an image of moving through the liquid world with confidence as our eyes are fixed on our Lord, who remains our solid foundation.

“There’s a temptation to want to either embrace or reject liquidity, which is a distraction,” says Franks, who believes “that we should be focused on embracing Christ and rejecting sin and in relying on him to give us the strength to move with confidence through difficult times.”

This, she believes, “is a great gift we can give to contemporary seekers, and hopefully help straighten out any possibly off-kilter priorities with the hope that they will be guided into the arms of the church.”

The panel presentations are available on YouTube beginning at 2:40.

author: Daniel Lipinski
title: Did Democrats Really Find a Religious Left?
original_title: Did Democrats Really Find a Religious Left?
summary:

The post Did Democrats Really Find a Religious Left? appeared first on First Things.
full_content:
Democrats won a string of midterm victories across the country, many of them unexpected. One popular narrative to emerge from the results is captured in this Wall Street Journal headline: “After Decades of a Religious Right, Democrats Find a Religious Left.” 

James Talarico, a Presbyterian (PCUSA) seminarian, will be the first Democratic senator elected in Texas since the 1980s. Adam Hamilton, a Methodist (UMC) megachurch pastor, will be the first Democratic senator from Kansas in more than eighty-five years. In addition, Sarah Trone Garriott, an ELCA pastor, and Lindsay James, a PCUSA minister, each flipped a House seat from Republican to Democrat in Iowa. All four of these candidates—three ordained ministers and a seminarian—cited Christ’s call to care for the poor as their primary motivation for supporting the Democratic policy agenda. 

If you had told me a year ago that the Democratic Party would have a number of candidates in major congressional races who centered their campaigns on their Christian ministry, I would have been shocked. If you had further revealed that the entire party would rally around these candidates and that they would pull off historic wins, I would have been incredulous. 

Something startling happened, yes. But it wasn’t the birth of a “religious left” counterpart to the “religious right.” Despite commentators affixing the broad label, what they are really referring to is the white mainline Protestant left. All four of these successful candidates come from churches that are theologically and politically liberal, the types of churches that were prominent in the Social Gospel movement that arose at the end of the nineteenth century. At that time, these churches and denominations were the largest, wealthiest, and most culturally powerful institutions in the country and had significant influence in the progressive movement. They were successful in setting up private institutions and advocating for government assistance to address social problems such as poverty, poor public health, and lax worker protections. 

While Senator-elect Hamilton has an enormous congregation in his own church, mainline denominations continue to shed members and are a faint shadow of what they used to be. These are not institutions that are presently capable of bringing about and supporting a potent new political movement. There is no indication that widespread organized action occurred at the grassroots level across these churches in this election. Nothing happened that demonstrated the rise of a movement comparable to the “religious right,” which influences tens of millions of voters and has an extensive grassroots network. 

The victorious campaigns of these candidates do suggest, however, that some potentially significant changes may be afoot in the Democratic Party and in American politics. Over the years, the Democratic Party became largely captured by anti-religionists who assert that religious faith must be kept out of the public square. The main reason these candidates received so much attention is that it is highly unusual for someone who highlights their Christian ministry (and is not black) to make it through a Democratic primary election and be widely embraced in the party. That all four did suggests anti-religionists had already lost some of their power. Now that these candidates have won and become political heroes, the party has an incentive to make more room for those who speak openly about their Christian faith. 

That receptiveness is likely to be limited, at least at first. After all, none of these candidates stepped far out of line, if at all, on the Democratic issue agenda. It will be another matter when a faithful candidate’s convictions lead somewhere the party doesn’t want to go. But it will be welcome progress if the party begins to rid itself of the intolerance shown to those who speak about the primacy of their faith in guiding their politics. This is a necessary first step if there is any hope of returning the Democratic Party to the position it held not long ago, when abortion was considered an issue of conscience and those who supported pro-life policies were accepted. 

Outside of the party, the fact that Democratic senators and representatives are forthrightly speaking about how their Christian faith calls them to be active in politics should help quiet the anti-religionists. Hopefully this will dispel the prejudice against voices of faith in the public square and allow us to return to the kind of open debate that our nation desperately needs. 

These victories will also likely draw more liberal Christians into politics. When something new succeeds in politics, others are bound to follow suit. The downside of this will be more candidates who make false Christian claims, such as James Talarico’s ghastly interpretation of the Annunciation as proof of God’s support for abortion. 

Our disgust over such statements, however, should not stop us from giving credit to these candidates for proclaiming and demonstrating some of Jesus’s foundational teachings. In the midst of an incredibly brutal campaign, when Talarico was asked by an interviewer whether he loved his opponent, Ken Paxton, he said, “Yes, [because] Ken Paxton is a child of God. He is my brother in Christ.” The placard on the rostrum from which he gave his victory speech on election night simply read “Love Thy Neighbor.” It is my profound hope that these and other examples of Christian witness we saw in this election will give courage to others to do the same. 

The midterm elections may have ushered in a big shift, one especially consequential for Christians. But it is probably not the one that mainstream observers would have us think.
